text: ,14 and some consider enteral nutrition the first choice of manage- ment in paediatric patients with Crohn’s disease.3 Combining an elemental diet with low-dose corticosteroids has also been sug- gested as a therapeutic approach in children, although it is as yet untested.14 Adult patients with Crohn’s disease who are consid- ered candidates for enteral nutrition include those on potentially high cumulative corticosteroid doses, or who are corticosteroid- refractory or corticosteroid-intolerant, or those at high risk for osteoporosis.5 Data are considered insufficient to assess the efficacy of enteral nutrition in ulcerative colitis.5,7 The term elemental diet was originally coined to describe diets containing free amino acids and glucose and was often prefixed by the phrase ‘chemically defined’. However, it came to embrace diets whose nitrogen sources included peptides and were often also called predigested diets. It was suggested15 that the term el- emental diet could be used for either type but that for those with an amino acid nitrogen source the term chemically defined ele- mental diet should be used whereas for those with a peptide nitrogen source predigested elemental diet was suitable. The term polymeric diet should be used for those diets with a whole protein nitrogen source (such as milk or soya). There appears to be little difference between formulas in terms of therapeutic response, although compliance may be better with polymeric feeds due to the unpalatability of elemental diets.3,5,13 Several different elemental diets are available; some contain long-chain triglycerides as the fat source, but for patients with impaired fat digestion, medium-chain triglycerides are consid- ered preferable.1 There is some suggestion that the effectiveness of enteral diets in treating active Crohn’s disease might relate to the fat rather than nitrogen composition,1,3,7 with less inflamma- tion occurring with those containing the fewest long-chain trig- lycerides.1 Other potentially beneficial components of diets for Crohn’s dis- ease include omega-3 triglycerides, which may have beneficial effects on inflammatory processes, and in achieving remis- sion;4,14,16 no clinical benefit has been seen with fatty acid or dietary fish oil supplementation in active ulcerative colitis.17 Short-chain fatty acids have been proposed as a means of in- creasing butyrate levels, which may have a direct anti-inflamma- tory effect on the colon; butyrate enemas have shown benefit in ulcerative colitis.5,13,17 The use of a substrate (‘pre-biotic’) to de- liver short-chain fatty acids, or directly delivering probiotics to the intestine, have also been proposed.5,17 Glutamine has been suggested as being beneficial for epithelial
